title: Strong absolute form of Mertens' First Theorem via a key identity
intent: Prove the absolute bound ℳ(n) − ln n ∈ (−1 − 9/π², ln 4] by routing the target remainder through one key identity ℳ n − ln n = ln (fact n) / n − ln n + r / n − R / n, so that three already-proved project lemmas bound the three terms on the right and a single transitivity step closes the interval.

parent.name: mertens_bound_strong
parent.statement:
theorem mertens_bound_strong:
  fixes n :: nat assumes n: "n > 0"
  shows   "\<MM> n - ln n \<in> {-1 - 9 / pi\<^sup>2<..ln 4}"

children.name: mertens_remainder_aux_bound
children.statement:
lemma mertens_remainder_aux_bound:
  fixes x :: real
  defines "R \<equiv> (\<Sum>(p,i) | prime p \<and> i > 1 \<and> real (p ^ i) \<le> x. ln (real p) / p ^ i)"
  shows   "R < 9 / pi\<^sup>2"
children.closed_by: finally show ?thesis by simp (the last estimate uses deriv_zeta_2_bound)
children.note: Analyst's paraphrase, replaced by the declaration's text: the prime-power remainder R = ∑ ln p / p^i over p prime, i > 1, p^i ≤ x is < 9/π²

children.name: primepows_le_subset
children.statement:
lemma primepows_le_subset:
  assumes x: "x > 0" and l: "l > 0"
  shows   "{(p, i). prime p \<and> l \<le> i \<and> real (p ^ i) \<le> x} \<subseteq> {..nat \<lfloor>root l x\<rfloor>} \<times> {..nat \<lfloor>log 2 x\<rfloor>}"
children.closed_by: proof safe … qed (two goals, each closed by auto/intro)
children.note: Analyst's paraphrase, replaced by the declaration's text: the prime powers {(p,i) | prime p ∧ l ≤ i ∧ p^i ≤ x} lie in a finite rectangle

children.name: ln_fact_conv_sum_upto_mangoldt
children.statement:
lemma ln_fact_conv_sum_upto_mangoldt:
  "ln (fact n) = sum_upto (\<lambda>k. mangoldt k * (n div k)) n"
children.note: Analyst's paraphrase, replaced by the declaration's text: ln (fact n) = sum_upto (λk. mangoldt k * (n div k)) n

children.name: \<theta>_upper_bound
children.statement:
lemma \<theta>_upper_bound:
  assumes x: "x \<ge> 1"
  shows   "\<theta> x < ln 4 * x"
children.note: Analyst's paraphrase, replaced by the declaration's text: θ x < ln 4 * x for x ≥ 1

children.name: sum_upto_primepows
children.statement:
lemma sum_upto_primepows:
  fixes f :: "nat \<Rightarrow> 'a :: comm_monoid_add"
  assumes "\<And>n. \<not>primepow n \<Longrightarrow> f n = 0" "\<And>p i. prime p \<Longrightarrow> i > 0 \<Longrightarrow> f (p ^ i) = g p i"
  shows   "sum_upto f x = (\<Sum>(p, i) | prime p \<and> i > 0 \<and> real (p ^ i) \<le> x. g p i)"
children.closed_by: finally show ?thesis . (via sum.reindex_bij_witness over p ↦ (p, multiplicity))
children.note: Analyst's paraphrase, replaced by the declaration's text: sum_upto f x = ∑ g p i over prime powers (p, i) with i > 0, p^i ≤ x, when f vanishes off prime powers

applicability.goal_shape: An absolute (not asymptotic) bound on a remainder of the form ℳ(n) − ln n, or more generally a sum over primes, that must hold on the whole domain, expressed as an interval membership ∈ (a, b].
applicability.use_when: The target quantity can be rewritten through one key identity into a few terms, each of which is bounded by a named lemma that was proved independently (here: log factorial via Stirling, a Chebyshev θ bound, and the prime-power remainder R); the combination of the estimates is a short transitivity step.
applicability.avoid_when: Only an asymptotic (Big-O) bound is needed, where the careful absolute estimates are overkill; or the terms are not genuinely independent so the leaves cannot be proved before the parent is assembled; or the key identity itself needs a non-trivial proof that dominates the work.

consequences: The move creates two kinds of obligation. First, the small cases (n = 1 and n = 2) must be closed by direct arithmetic, outside the key identity. Second, each of the three terms the identity exposes must be bounded into a non-negative interval of the right width, so that their combination via the identity lands in the target interval: R/n ∈ [0, 9/π²), r/n ∈ [0, ln 4), and ln n − ln(fact n)/n ∈ [0, 1]. Failure mode: if any one estimate is not tight enough or has the wrong sign, the final `with ... by simp` no longer closes the interval, and the whole theorem must be re-proved around a tighter bound.
